q: My supplier is a GST composition dealer and gives a bill of supply. Can I use it as carbon evidence?
title: Bill of supply as carbon evidence
short: Yes, if it shows what was supplied and how much. A bill of supply is a valid GST document from a composition dealer, but quantity is often missing from it. If it gives only an amount, get the delivery challan or weighbridge slip for the quantity, or use a spend-based estimate labelled as such.
audience: MSME buyers of fuel, materials and services from small suppliers

sections.h: Why your supplier issues a bill of supply
p: A registered supplier who pays tax under the composition scheme, or who supplies only exempt goods or services, issues a bill of supply instead of a tax invoice. A composition dealer cannot charge GST, so the bill shows no tax and you claim no input credit on it.

sections.h: What the bill will and will not show
ul: Supplier name, address and GSTIN, a serial number and the date.
Your details if you are registered, a description of the goods or service, the HSN or SAC code and the value.
Quantity is not something to count on. Many bills print it; many give only a description and a rupee amount.
For the full list of required contents, read Rule 49 of the CGST Rules on the CBIC website.

ol: Description and HSN tell you the material or fuel.
Quantity and unit, if printed, are your activity data. Multiply by a published factor.
If no quantity, match the bill to the delivery challan, weighbridge slip, gate entry or stock register for the same date.
If nothing gives a quantity, use the amount for a spend-based estimate and label it so.

sections.h: How strong is it as evidence
p: A bill of supply comes from a registered supplier and carries their GSTIN, so it can be traced back to them. Do not rely on your GSTR-2B to confirm it, since that statement is built for input tax credit, which a bill of supply does not give. Keep the paper or PDF and the payment record together.

example.title: Worked example: coal from a composition dealer
lines: Bill of supply: coal, HSN 2701, ₹42,000, no quantity printed
Weighbridge slip, same date and vehicle: 3,500 kg net
Emissions: 3,500 x 2.42 kg CO2 per kg = 8,470 kg CO2, about 8.5 t, Scope 1 if burnt on site
example.note: The coal factor is the IPCC 2006 default used by Senseible. The quantity comes from the weighbridge slip, not the rupee amount.

senseible: Senseible reads a bill of supply like any other invoice. When a line prints a quantity it applies the published factor; when it does not, the line shows Needs Data until a delivery document gives the quantity, or Senseible provides a spend-based estimate labelled with wider uncertainty.
